Hi @kinghuang!

This is currently working as intended (semantically, we didn't want to consider the initial render of a widget a change to it), and I believe that most implementations of callbacks (for example, javascript `onchange` handlers) follow the same convention.

I can, however, see how needing to special-case the initial state to have certain things run could be a pain depending on your use case. This may be a tricky one as I'd imagine that changing the behavior to call the callback on first render would similarly make other use cases have to write some code to special-case the first run and avoid doing things.

For now, I think our path forward for this issue will be to wait a bit to see how often people bring up this problem, and we can reevaluate our decision after collecting a bit more data as either solution will come with its own caveats.

While that does match how an `onChange` handler on an html `<select>` element would behave, I'd argue that it's not the right call for Streamlit, especially as part of the State API.

The programming model for Streamlit's interactive widgets is purely data oriented. When a widget like [`st.selectbox`](https://docs.streamlit.io/en/stable/session_state_api.html) is called, the return value is the widget's value not an instance of the widget. Developers don't get to interact with the widget object itself.

With the State API, widget values can now be backed by session state. As part of the State API and in keeping with Streamlit's data oriented flow, I believe that `on_change` should be called for changes to the state value, not changes to the widget value. So, when a widget sets a state value from *nothing* to the initial/default value, that is a change to the state value which should trigger `on_change`. Since developers don't have access to the widget, having `on_change` be based on widget changes is not as useful.

Or, put another way, I should be able to transpose Streamlit code that acts on the return value of a widget into an `on_change` function, and have it do the same thing. As it stands, the transposed code will miss the first value. And, I now have to capture the return value and figure out how to call the `on_change` handler *just the first time*, which doesn't seem right for a Streamlit app.

**Example code:**

The same logical code that acts on a widget's return value and `on_change` produces different results. The `on_change` handler isn't aware of the widget's initial value.

```python
import streamlit as st

if not "initialized" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.return_values = []
    st.session_state.change_values = []
    st.session_state.initialized = True

def capture_change_value():
    st.session_state.change_values.append(st.session_state.number)
    st.text(f"Change values: {st.session_state.change_values}")

def capture_return_value(number):
    st.session_state.return_values.append(number)
    st.text(f"Return values: {st.session_state.return_values}")

capture_return_value(st.number_input("Number", key="number", on_change=capture_change_value))
```

**Output after clicking + three times:**

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/27340/126874503-ac0ce0e9-e891-4b47-8260-6c8fc685a9ba.png)

**Example workaround:**

In order for existing code to work in an `on_change` handler, you'd have to capture the return value of a widget and call the `on_change` handler manually, but only for the very first return value. This isn't in keeping with Streamlit's data-oriented and not widget-oriented programming model.

```python
import streamlit as st

if not "initialized" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.return_values = []
    st.session_state.change_values = []
    st.session_state.initialized = True
    st.session_state.first_return = True

def capture_change_value():
    st.session_state.change_values.append(st.session_state.number)
    st.text(f"Change values: {st.session_state.change_values}")

def capture_return_value(number):
    if st.session_state.first_return:
        capture_change_value()
        st.session_state.first_return = False

    st.session_state.return_values.append(number)
    st.text(f"Return values: {st.session_state.return_values}")

capture_return_value(st.number_input("Number", key="number", on_change=capture_change_value))
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/27340/126874666-c96d361c-e7b6-416d-b41a-8f952974f2e7.png)

Here's another example of the problem, which requires even more complexity to solve. For a selectbox, if the options change, the `on_change` handler is not called for the first selection of the changed options.

```python
import streamlit as st

list_one = ("One", ("A", "B", "C"))
list_two = ("Two", ("D", "E", "F"))

if not "initialized" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.return_values = []
    st.session_state.change_values = []
    st.session_state.initialized = True

def capture_change_value():
    st.session_state.change_values.append(st.session_state.item)
    st.text(f"Change values: {st.session_state.change_values}")

def capture_return_value(item):
    st.session_state.return_values.append(item)
    st.text(f"Return values: {st.session_state.return_values}")

ret1 = st.selectbox("List", (list_one, list_two), key="list", format_func=lambda x: x[0])
ret2 = st.selectbox("Item", st.session_state.list[1], key="item", format_func=lambda x: x, on_change=capture_change_value)

capture_return_value(ret2)
```

Starting with `A` (the initial value), then selecting `B`, and `C` from the **Item** selectbox, then selecting **List** `Two` and continuing with `D`, `E` and `F` results in the `on_change` handler only being called for `B`, `C`, `E`, `F`. The two initial/default values, `A` and `D`, are missed and would require special handling.

Hi @kinghuang : I'm on the Product team at Streamlit. First of all, I want to say that we appreciate your efforts in bringing up this issue.

While the examples you share help illustrate the problem, we would love to learn more about your use case for requesting a callback to be called when a widget sets the initial/default value. Can you shed some light on the app you're trying to build and if you've tried any workarounds to get around the problem?

Sure, I don't have time to whip up a full example app right now, but I'll try to describe the main bits.

I'm currently using Streamlit to build a series of review apps for our spaCy NLP pipelines. Using the new State API, I've been storing a database session object, a batch of rows for review, and a process object (basically a controller for what's being reviewed). Central to the apps are custom Streamlit components for doing things like scoring the quality of the Doc objects or modifying labels in the entity spans in the Doc objects.

Here's an abbreviated version of the function that is struggling with the `on_change` calls.

```python
def process_and_batch_selector(process_title="Process", batch_title="Batch"):
    # Prepare data change handlers.
    def process_changed():
        st.session_state.batch_infos = st.session_state.process.batch_infos()

    def batch_changed():
        batch_info = st.session_state.batch_info
        if not batch_info:
            return

        # When a batch changes, commit any pending changes in the active session,
        # then create a new session for the batch.
        if session := st.session_state.session:
            session.commit()
            session.close()

        st.session_state.session = session = create_session()

        # Get the batch id from batch_info, and load a full object for the batch
        # into the session.
        process = st.session_state.process
        batch_id = batch_info[0]

        st.session_state.batch = session.query(process.batch_cls).filter(process.batch_cls.id == batch_id).first()

    # Initialize session state data.
    if not "session" in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.session = None
        st.session_state.batch = None

    # Select the review process.
    if process_title:
        st.subheader(process_title)
    process = st.selectbox("", PROCESSES, format_func=lambda p: p.label, key="process", on_change=process_changed)

    # Workaround for selectbox state and on_change limitations
    if not "batch_infos" in st.session_state:
        process_changed()

    if batch_title:
        st.subheader(batch_title)
    batch_info = st.selectbox("", st.session_state.batch_infos, format_func=lambda info: info[1], key="batch_info", on_change=batch_changed)

    # Workaround for selectbox state and on_change limitations
    if batch_info is not None and st.session_state.session is None:
        batch_changed()
```

When a `batch_info` is selected, I want to commit changes in the batch being edited (if any), then fetch the new batch of objects from the database for editing.

If you look for the `# Workaround` comments, you can see where the `on_change` functions are being explicitly invoked for both process and batch selection. Without them, the initial/default batch that is selected doesn't load, for example, because the batch selectbox's `on_change` function isn't called.

If I didn't set the `key` attribute on the batch selector on the batch selectbox and relied on its return value, I would get the value (including the initial/default value) on every run of the code. But, then, I'd have to implement my own change detection, probably by storing a value in `session_state` and then comparing it to the return value.

Hi @BrtSnsn , it was hard to debug this but I was able to do it with the help of my coworker. Sorry for the late reply. 

It looks like the bug is being caused by `datetime.now()` because datetime.now() is constantly changing. Just some context: Streamlit works by completely rerunning the script and keeping track of widget ids and those widget ids are a hash of the specific parameters. With that context given, because datetime.now() is always changing, that causes those widgets ids to change and as a result, the session state is not being kept. 

What would probably work is changing the time to the day, hour, or minute of `datetime.now()`  depending on your usecase. Based on the architecture of this system, I'm not sure we can exactly solve the datetime.now() issue anytime soon given the architecture of streamlit but I plan to make a PR that suggests to users to not use `datetime.now()` and maybe use the day or hour because of this issue. 

Sorry if this inconveniences you but thanks for submitting this issue. Happy streamlitting!

Hi @kmcgrady,

Personally I've been aware of this for a long time and while I understand that this is a design decision, I have never understood the rationale for this particular choice.

One reason why I do not like it is that passing `key` to the widget is an explicit attempt to save the widget state in the session state. It is a very convenient syntactic sugar for associating widgets with explicit updates to `st.session_state` - or it would be, except it does not actually do that and it's not very upfront about that fact.

Personally, if the widget has been declared with the `key`, it usually means that I want to keep the state independently of whether the widget is currently displayed or not. Sometimes I do not care. And although I can certainly imagine valid reasons why someone would want the state to go away with the widget, I have never wanted it to, and if I did, I would prefer to explicitly clear the state anyway.

The fact that the saving is conditional on the widget being there and that fact is not very explicitly sign-posted in the description of the `key` parameter is very confusing to newcomers. I do not think it is much of an overstatement to say that on https://discuss.streamlit.io/ there is a thread about "why am I losing my widget state?" every other day.

For those of us who do know about it it results in code littered with callback functions which serve only the purpose of running the 'fake' widget session state into the 'real' persistent widget state.

I think the bottom line with this is that the way Streamlit state works now, there are three modes:

1. transient (normal widgets)
2. persistent (`st.session_state`)
3. persistent, but only sometimes (widget session state)

The existence of the third one is, in my opinion, not very useful.

Objectively, it is poorly documented. The [Session State API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/session-state) treats the two like as if they were the same thing:

>Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:

The [Multipage Apps](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/get-started/multipage-apps) site explicitly says:

>Pages share the same [st.session_state](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/session-state):

The linked page says:

>Session State provides the functionality to store variables across reruns. Widget state (i.e. the value of a widget) is also stored in a session.

>For simplicity, we have unified this information in one place. i.e. the Session State. This convenience feature makes it super easy to read or write to the widget's state anywhere in the app's code. Session State variables mirror the widget value using the key argument.

This hints at the fact that the two are different, but never properly explains the caveats of using the widget state. The only place that does is the [Advanced notes on widget behaviour](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/widget-semantics):

>If you don't call a widget function in a script run, we neither store the widget state nor render the widget. If you call a widget function with the same arguments later, Streamlit treats it as a new widget.

While updating the documentation to really drive home the real behavior could be one solution, I would argue that whoever wrote the documentation described how this process would work in an intuitive manner: *if you put the `key` on a widget, the state will be saved in `st.session.state`, which persists between pages*, and it's the real behavior that is counter-intuitive.

Hi @MathijsNL, thanks for reporting this! This is a bit of a weird one because, in some ways, I'd argue the bug exactly as described here is expected behavior, but there's a different/related bug that we'll certainly want to fix.

This behavior started in version 1.18.0 and is due to one of my recent changes (https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/5856) that keeps a session around for ~2 minutes after a browser tab is closed. The reason this was done was to make session state resilient to transient websocket disconnects (most often caused by a short network blip) that would previously cause session state to randomly be reset for no apparent reason.

When the browser tab is closed, session state from that point on is inaccessible to the user since there's no way to reconnect to that session from that point. Ideally, that's the mental model we would like to allow people to have even if the actual session cleanup is deferred, so I'm not inclined to change the docs to include the nitty-gritty details of delayed cleanup.

The bug from my point of view is that I didn't take into account scripts that may keep running when the browser tab is closed (script execution is at latest stopped when we delete the session, so this would always happen close to immediately before #5856 was released). Ideally, script execution should stop once we've detected that the corresponding browser tab has been closed (technically, it'd stop at the next `st.*` command as we're not able to preempt it earlier). I wouldn't expect a developer to have to think about this and manually handle script lifecycle via session state. Would implementing a fix to have the script stop running on websocket connection close work for your use case?

I'll try to get a fix out for this (that stops script execution on websocket disconnect) sometime in the next few weeks, but in the meantime, any Streamlit version below 1.18.0 shouldn't have this issue if downgrading is possible.

What's likely going on here is that stopping the script run calls the internal method [ScriptRunner.request_stop](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/3626677888773768a82b44edd5092cbbcc0f2e6b/lib/streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner.py#L190), which disconnects the session state to guard against a potential race condition where two `ScriptRunner`s are simultaneously mutating the same session state object. Your `asyncio` coroutines then try to access the `st.session_state` object and hit the `AttributeError`.

I think I'd consider this issue as falling somewhere on the border between a bug report and a feature request since our `ScriptRunner` infrastructure doesn't take into account ways that an app session's state can be asynchronously mutated by the user script. Support for this would probably require a good deal of work to reevaluate our assumptions around where async session state mutations can come from, and it's unlikely that we'd prioritize doing this without a significant increase in demand for supporting this from the community (I think these types of use-cases are relatively uncommon).

For now, I'd recommend the workaround (which is obvious enough that I'm sure you've already considered it) of having your coroutines exit early if expected session state keys disappear since that implies that the script has stopped.

Hi @Mow17, When you assign a key ('input') to a widget, Streamlit will check session state when that widget function is executed. If it sees that key already exists, Streamlit will try to assign the value `st.session_state.input` to the widget having `key='input'`. That causes an error if the data type or format saved in session state cannot be parsed for that widget. In this case, trying to assign a value of `[]` to `st.text_area` is not understood by Streamlit. If you set `key='data'` for `st.text_area` in both examples, then `good()` would cause the error and `bad()` would work. I think the error message is a little less clear for `st.text_area`, so here's a clearer example: ```python import streamlit as st if 'my_key' not in st.session_state: st.session_state.my_key='a' st.number_input('A', key='my_key') ``` I agree that the error message for `st.text_area` is a little less than obvious, so it would be nice if that could made clearer. 😄 P.S. There are indeed several words that exist as methods you would not want to overwrite, but I don't think 'input' is one of them. If you're interested, here's a very short Streamlit script that can show you what's built it: ```python import streamlit as st st.write(dir(st.session_state)) ```

Just a bit of experimentation around Streamlit, threads, and asyncio.

My understanding:
- Every time a re-render is required (state change, user interaction, etc), a new thread is created and the script is run fresh. The old thread, if it hasn't already completed the script, may keep going (due to fastRerun) but any interaction with st objects will throw a Shutdown Exception.
- Streamlit does not care about asyncio, rather only if the thread has terminated or not.

I'm not sure how scalable this is -- threads will be active for each user potentially -- but my approach has been:
- Use asyncio.run() at the end of the script. This will create a new event loop for the thread (and render).
- The asyncio loop has tasks, which may run forever, *must* frequently interact with st (e.g. st.session_state) to trigger potential Shutdown exceptions to clean up the threads.
- If the asyncio loop ends early, then the "Running" indicator stops. So you can see the thread is still busy.

I haven't done scaled testing, but this approach seems to be working sensibly in my tests.

Hi, I've found a way to combine threading & fragment to get a fairly responsive behavior.

```
import time
from functools import wraps
from threading import Thread

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

import streamlit as st
from streamlit.runtime.scriptrunner import add_script_run_ctx, get_script_run_ctx


## function wrapper
def run_in_thread(func):
    # per https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76472211/multithreading-for-streamlit-and-kite-connect
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        thread = Thread(target=func, args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
        ctx = get_script_run_ctx()
        add_script_run_ctx(thread, ctx)
        thread.start()
    return wrapper


# this is a fn that takes time to complete, (e.g. database call, etc.)
# so we run it in a thread
@run_in_thread
def generate_data(x=1, sleep=2):  # example from j.carroll
    print('in generate data fn')
    time.sleep(sleep)  # simulating the delay
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        np.random.randn(5, 5) * x, columns=["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
    )
    print(f'returning df after sleep.. len={len(df)}')
    st.session_state.df = df


LOAD_FREQ = 10
@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def update_data():
    print('in update data fn')
    load_timer = st.session_state.load_timer
    now = time.monotonic()
    if now > load_timer + LOAD_FREQ:
        # avoid generating data all the time
        print('update data now > timer + freq')
        st.session_state.load_timer = now
        generate_data()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)
def filter_data(min_idx):
    print('in filter data fn')
    df = st.session_state.df
    st.session_state.df_f = df[df.index >= min_idx].copy()


@st.fragment(run_every=1)

    print('in draw graph fn')
    df = st.session_state.df_f
    if df is not None:
        graph_slot.plotly_chart(px.bar(df))

        st.session_state.df = pd.DataFrame()
        st.session_state.df_f = pd.DataFrame()
    if 'load_timer' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.load_timer = time.monotonic()

    st.button("Button 1")
```

Having done a bunch of experimentation myself I have a few things to add.  There is a lot of inaccurate information floating around on the web about this subject.  The really important thing to remember is what's mentioned in the comment by @mescanne above:

> Every time a re-render is required (state change, user interaction, etc), a new thread is created and the script is run fresh. The old thread, if it hasn't already completed the script, may keep going (due to fastRerun) but any interaction with st objects will throw a Shutdown Exception.

This means that whlie you can use `asyncio.run()` in your script (the [Medium post](https://sehmi-conscious.medium.com/got-that-asyncio-feeling-f1a7c37cab8b) unfortunately linked from Streamlit's own documentation falsely claims otherwise), you can't allow any interaction with your app while the event loop is running, and any tasks you launch on it can't reliably access `st.` functions for the reasons mentioned above.  It will also lead to a possibly large number of threads being created since, as mentioned above, the resulting asyncio event loop may run forever.

While you can manually create an event loop, set it for the current thread, and recover it on future invocations of your script **in that same thread**, this isn't particularly useful because your script code may or may not (actually won't, probably) run on that thread.  You also can't, for example, call `run_until_complete` on the event loop for [well-known reasons](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/66435).

Also, despite what said Medium post claims, calling `asyncio.get_running_loop` **definitely does not** return Streamlit's own event loop, as it will always be on a different thread than the one that runs your script.  This is, of course, what this bug is actually about :-)  If you don't care about security, reliability, stability, etc, and you don't want to call `st.` functions from your tasks, you can get it by calling `_get_async_objs()` on the session runtime.  For instance:

```python
import asyncio
import time
import streamlit as st

loop = st.runtime.get_instance()._get_async_objs().eventloop

async def do_nothing(seconds):
    await asyncio.sleep(3)
    print("HELLO WORLD", seconds)

if st.button(label="Do something"):
    loop.create_task(do_nothing(time.time()))

if st.button(label="Do something else"):
    st.toast("Hello!")
```

The best workaround for the moment, if you need to use asyncio for something, is probably to explicitly create a separate thread to run asyncio tasks, using `add_script_run_ctx` to give it access to the session state so that it can communicate with the rest of the UI.

I also don't really see how a solution to this problem could easily be implemented in Streamlit.  Conceptually, what is necessary, is what the original poster's "ugly workaround" is supposed to do, and what the Medium post claims Streamlit does, but which neither of them actually do, namely creating (possibly on demand) an event loop for each session context which script code can use to launch tasks.  Why this doesn't work:

- Simply creating an event loop doesn't actually start it!  So calling `create_task` on said loop will not do anything at all.
- Running an event loop is a blocking, non-reentrant operation.   Obviously a Streamlit `AppContext` (which runs in the main thread) can't do this.   But also a Streamlit `ScriptRunner` (which runs in its own thread) can't do this either, because there could be any number of threads for a given session context.

I don't claim to really understand Streamlit's architecture but it seems like a possible implementation woud be to create a separate thread for each script context, run an event loop there, and somehow give script code access to this event loop so that it can create and wait on tasks launched in it.  The evil solution would be to do magic on `await` in script code to make it do that ;-)

- Any running tasks will do ... something undefined, I think ... if you stop the event loop, and Python will complain about this.

This issue reports that when a WebSocket connection closes uncleanly (e.g., due to network disruptions), Streamlit creates a new session instead of reconnecting to the existing one, causing users to lose their session state.

**Root cause analysis:** The issue originates in `lib/streamlit/runtime/websocket_session_manager.py` in the `connect_session()` method. When a client attempts to reconnect with an existing session ID, the code checks if that session is already in `_active_session_info_by_id` (line 103). If it is, a warning is logged ("Session with id %s is already connected!") and a **new** session is created instead. The session can only be restored from storage if it's NOT currently active.

The core problem is a race condition: on an unclean WebSocket close, the server may not have detected the disconnect yet, so the session remains "active" in memory. When the client quickly reconnects with the same session ID, the server sees it as "already connected" and creates a new session instead of allowing reconnection. A potential fix would need to handle this case by either closing the existing connection first, implementing a grace period, or using a different strategy for tracking active vs. disconnected sessions.

Hey all — this issue has been on my radar and I wanted to share some design thinking. Sharing it here since this issue already captures the problem well and I'd love to get reactions.

### The idea: `st.background_task`

A managed API for kicking off long-running work that survives reruns:

```python
task = st.background_task(slow_query, args=(params,), key="my_query")

if task.running:
    st.info("Query running...")
elif task.done:
    st.dataframe(task.result)
```

The `key` deduplicates across reruns (same key = same task, not a new one). When the task finishes, the runtime automatically triggers a rerun so you can render the result — no polling needed. Tasks get cleaned up when the session ends.

The workaround @mkleinbort-ic shared above with raw threads works, but threads created outside Streamlit don't have access to `ScriptRunContext`, can't trigger reruns on completion, and aren't tied to the session lifecycle. This would handle all of that.

### How it relates to parallel fragments

We're working on `@st.fragment(parallel=True)` ([#14277](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14277)) which gives concurrency *within* a single script run — independent UI sections load at the same time. Background tasks would be different: the work outlives reruns, produces data rather than UI, and doesn't block interactions. They'd be complementary.

- Does the API shape feel right? The original proposal here used a decorator (`@st.run_in_background`) — any preference?
- What are your actual use cases? Long queries, model training, batch jobs?
- How important is cancellation when inputs change?

This is a **bug / upstream-dependency regression**. Streamlit's `lib/pyproject.toml` currently declares `websockets>=12.0.0,<17`, which still allows `websockets` to resolve to **16.1** (released 2026-07-09). - **websockets 16.1** — `http11.py`: `value = raw_value.decode("iso-8859-1")` → `é` becomes the real char `U+00E9`, which uvicorn's surrogateescape re-encode **cannot** encode → `UnicodeEncodeError` → handshake aborts. ❌

(16.1's `parse_headers` docstring still claims *"Non-ASCII characters are represented with surrogate escapes,"* which no longer matches its own code — worth flagging upstream.)

### Two corrections/notes for triage

1. **Dependency constraint.** The current constraint (both `develop` and 1.58.0) is `websockets>=12.0.0` with **no upper bound** — not `<17`. So 16.1 (and anything newer) is fully permitted, and fresh installs pull it.
2. **Workaround discrepancy resolved.** The reporter says pinning `websockets<16.1` fixes it; @chassotce says it didn't. In this exact stack (streamlit 1.58.0 / uvicorn 0.51.0), **`websockets==16.0` makes the non-ASCII handshake succeed** (101, no crash) — so the pin *does* work here. @chassotce's result was likely a different websockets/uvicorn combination (Authentik + Python 3.10/3.14).

### Possible Streamlit-side mitigations

- Add an upper bound / exclude the broken range in `lib/pyproject.toml` (e.g. `websockets>=12.0.0,!=16.1` or a tested cap), and/or
- Track the upstream fix — this is fundamentally a websockets 16.1 ↔ uvicorn incompatibility (uvicorn should re-encode with `latin-1` to preserve the ISO-8859-1 bytes websockets now produces).

This is a confirmed **regression** (works in `1.58.0`, crashes in every version from `1.59.0` onward). When a fragment calls `.status()` on a container declared *outside* the fragment and then opens that status block with two separate `with` statements, the app crashes to a blank page with `Uncaught Error: Cannot set a node at a delta path`.

**Root cause** (matches the reporter's excellent analysis): `StatusContainer._create` captures the delta path from the **parent cursor before** the block is created (`lib/streamlit/elements/lib/mutable_status_container.py:81-91`). Since `1.59.0`, a write from a fragment into an outside container is redirected into a per-fragment layout-transparent wrapper block, so the status (`expandable`) block actually lands one level deeper than the captured path predicted. The stale `_delta_path` therefore points at the `transparent` wrapper instead of the status. On the second `with`, `__exit__` calls `update(state="complete")`, which re-emits the status block directly at that stale path (`mutable_status_container.py:151`). On the frontend, `AppRoot.addBlock` only inherits the existing children when the block type matches (`frontend/lib/src/render-tree/AppRoot.ts:467-483`); `transparent` ≠ `expandable`, so the whole subtree is dropped and the next element is written to a path whose parent no longer exists, causing `SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor` to throw. Note the one-`with` variant silently corrupts the tree without a visible crash.

A promising fix is to capture `_delta_path` **after** `_block()` from the path it actually wrote to, rather than predicting it from the parent cursor beforehand; other elements that store a delta path and later enqueue a message with it directly should be audited too.

### Triage summary

This is a **dependency-compatibility bug** in Streamlit's web server, not a Community Cloud–specific problem — it affects any environment where a fresh install resolves Starlette to a newer release (Community Cloud just happens to auto-resolve the latest compatible versions).

**Root cause:** Streamlit's custom gzip middleware (`lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_gzip_middleware.py`) subclasses and directly instantiates Starlette's *internal* `GZipResponder`/`IdentityResponder` classes, which are private implementation details rather than public API:

```python
responder = _MediaAwareGZipResponder(
    self.app, self.minimum_size, compresslevel=self.compresslevel
)
```

`_MediaAwareGZipResponder` does not override `__init__`, so it inherits Starlette's constructor. A newer Starlette release changed `GZipResponder.__init__` to add a required keyword-only argument `thread_minimum_size`. Because the responder is instantiated without it, startup fails before any app code runs:

```
TypeError: GZipResponder.__init__() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'thread_minimum_size'
```

Streamlit's runtime dependency range in `lib/pyproject.toml` is `starlette>=0.46.0,<2`, so the incompatible Starlette version satisfies the upper bound (`<2`) and gets installed. This coupling to Starlette internals was introduced with the Starlette/Uvicorn server migration ([#14553](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14553)).

**Workaround confirmed by multiple reporters:** pin `starlette<1.4.0` (e.g. `starlette==1.3.1`) in `requirements.txt`.

**Suggested fix:** cap the Starlette upper bound below the breaking release (and/or make the middleware resilient to the changed responder signature, e.g. forward `thread_minimum_size` or stop relying on the private responder classes).

### Related Issues

- [#15378 – Running Streamlit with Starlette in Corporate Network](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15378): Another `area:server` bug stemming from the Starlette/Uvicorn migration; related to server behavior introduced by the same migration, though a different symptom (WebSocket connectivity).
- [#15022 – Intermittent `OSError: [WinError 121]` since upgrading to `v1.57.0`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/15022): Also traces back to the 1.57 Starlette/Uvicorn migration and touches the same server layer, indicating shared risk in the new Starlette stack.

No existing issue appears to be a duplicate of this specific `GZipResponder`/Starlette-version incompatibility.

This is a real Components V2 race, not identity churn and almost certainly not `_pending_resets`. With an explicit `key`, the element id stays stable (`key_as_main_identity=True`), but `useHandleJsContent` still re-runs the default export whenever `data` changes. A mount-time `setTriggerValue` then has to win a one-shot delivery race: the value is stored under the synthetic trigger-aggregator id (`$$STREAMLIT_INTERNAL_KEY_<id>__events`), flushed on `setTimeout(0)`, deleted from client widget state, and cleared again by `_reset_triggers()` at the end of every script run.

That aggregator id is not in the render tree, so `removeInactiveWidgetState()` on `ScriptFinished` can delete a pending trigger before the macrotask flush sends it. `_coalesce_widget_states` also preserves `trigger_value` / `chat_input_value` across queued reruns but not `json_trigger_value`, so a second widget-update message can overwrite a just-queued CCv2 trigger. Both fit the controls: `setStateValue` lives on the element id and persists; event-handler triggers fire after the app has settled. `_pending_resets` is page-scope persist-state tracking and is not involved in this repro.

Mount-time triggers are still a poor fit for Streamlit's model (use `setStateValue` for init data), but silent ~25% loss with a stable key is a bug, not intended discard-on-re-register.

This is a bug in `AppTest`, reproduced on Streamlit 1.64.0 and 1.65.0: a keyed widget with `persist_state="page"` keeps its value while hidden, then comes back empty when shown again, even though the test never changes pages. A browser session keeps the value, and `persist_state="session"` keeps it in `AppTest`. `AppTest._run()` builds a new `PagesManager` on every run, and that manager's current page hash starts as `""`. `ScriptRunner` compares that empty hash with the target page (the main-script hash when no page was requested), treats the rerun as a page change, and runs page-change widget cleanup before `ScriptRunContext.reset()` installs the real page hash. Page-scoped persistence then sees a different page and drops the preserved value, including the pending reset that makes the remounted widget ignore its stored value. A contributor reproduced this on `develop`; seeding the new manager with the requested hash stops the false page change, but that also makes the current and requested hashes identical after `switch_page()`, so the pre-run cleanup that should drop page-scoped state before the new page registers widgets would be skipped. The seed needs to be the page from the previous run, with the requested hash passed separately.
